case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 7-year-old boy was admitted to the hospital with 1 week of temperatures up to 40.2 °C (104.4 °F), productive cough, and lethargy, which did not improve after 3 days of oral cefuroxime. He lived in rural China and had close contact with dogs, cattle, and sheep. His blood pressure was 93/60 mm Hg; heart rate, 100/min; respiratory rate, 26/min; and oxygen saturation, 94% on room air. Lung auscultation revealed absent breath sounds on the right hemithorax. His abdomen was soft and nontender, without hepatosplenomegaly. His white blood cell count was 8000/μL, with 25.8% eosinophils (reference range, 0%-9%). C-reactive protein level and results from tuberculin skin test, interferon-γ release assay, nucleic acid amplification testing for tuberculosis, acid-fast bacilli smear microscopy, and HIV antibody testing were normal. A thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) scan showed a ruptured 10 × 9 × 5–cm right upper lobe pulmonary cyst compressing the right main bronchus and 3 liver cysts (Figure 1).

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain serologic testing forE granulosusantibodies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that cysts in the lung and liver are highly suggestive of cystic echinococcosis. Organ biopsy (choices C and D) is not recommended because of the risk of secondary spread of infection, and cyst content spillage may cause anaphylaxis. Choice A is incorrect because humans with cystic echinococcosis do not excreteE granulosuseggs in stool. Cystic echinococcosis is caused by infection with the larval stage of a tapeworm calledE granulosus. More than 1 million people annually are infected withE granulosusworldwide. Endemic regions include western China, Central Asia, South America, Mediterranean countries, and east Africa.1-3Cystic echinococcosis is rare in the US and typically occurs in immigrants from endemic countries.4 Definitive hosts forE granulosusare domestic or wild dogs and wolves (canids), who acquire the infection after eating animal organs containing hydatid cysts. Inside canids, the cysts develop into adult tapeworms, which shed eggs in their stool. Intermediate hosts, such as sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle, become infected after ingesting tapeworm eggs in contaminated soil.3Humans can become hosts through consumption of contaminated soil, food, or water, or after close contact with animal hosts.1After reaching the intestine,E granulosuseggs hatch and embryos penetrate the intestinal wall, migrating through blood or lymphatic vessels to organs, where they develop into hydatid cysts that gradually enlarge and produce more cysts.3,5 Approximately 70% of adults with cystic echinococcosis have liver cysts, and approximately 10% to 30% have pulmonary cysts.6In children, pulmonary cysts are the most common manifestation of cystic echinococcosis.7,8Less frequently, hyatid cysts develop in the brain, spleen, kidney, pancreas, and heart. Complications of cystic echinococcosis result from compression of adjacent organs, cyst rupture, superinfection, and immunoallergic reactions toEchinococcus, including urticaria, angioedema, and, rarely, anaphylaxis.8 Liver cysts typically grow slowly over many years in adults, but cysts often increase in size at a faster rate in the lung and in children.4,6,7Pulmonary cysts typically range from 1 cm to 20 cm, with giant cysts defined as having a diameter of 10 cm or greater.6Individuals with uncomplicated pulmonary hyatid cysts are typically asymptomatic, while those with complicated (ruptured or infected) cysts may experience cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, and fever.6Pulmonary cyst rupture can cause cough productive of salty-tasting fluid or membrane fragments, empyema, and hydropneumothorax.7 The diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis is made based on history, imaging, serology, and histology. Typical imaging findings are pulmonary cysts on chest radiographs or CT and liver cysts on abdominal ultrasound or CT. Detection of antibodies againstEchinococcuscan confirm the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis, although the sensitivity and specificity of serology each vary from 60% to 90%, and the sensitivity of serology is not well defined in children.4,7Eosinophilia occurs in approximately 25% of patients with confirmed cystic echinococcosis.9 Treatment for cystic echinococcosis depends on cyst size and location, presence or absence of complications, and availability of medical expertise and equipment.4Cure can be achieved by surgical resection of the cyst. Other treatments include PAIR (percutaneous puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration), antihelminth therapy, and watchful waiting for smaller cysts. Limited evidence is available regarding optimal drug therapy. However, albendazole or albendazole-praziquantel may be considered for patients with inoperable cysts in the liver, cysts in multiple organs, or isolated small or medium-sized cysts. Antihelminth therapy as an adjunct to surgery or interventional procedures decreased the risk of echinococcosis dissemination and recurrence.4,8,10Approximately 6.5% of patients experience a relapse after treatment for cystic echinococcosis.1 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay antibodies toEchinococcuswere detected, confirming the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis. Albendazole (15 mg/kg/d orally twice daily) was started 1 week before right upper lobectomy and continued for 5 months postoperatively. During surgery, a 12 × 12 × 8–cm pulmonary cyst was removed (Figure 2). Histopathology showed extensive necrosis and calcification, andE granulosuswas seen on hematoxylin and eosin stain. Five months after his initial surgery, the patient underwent laparotomy and complete removal of the 3 liver cysts, with no spillage of their contents. He was prescribed albendazole for 3 months postoperatively. When seen in the clinic 2 months after liver surgery, the patient had recovered well and an abdominal ultrasound showed no cyst recurrence.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain serologic testing forE granulosusantibodies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that cysts in the lung and liver are highly suggestive of cystic echinococcosis. Organ biopsy (choices C and D) is not recommended because of the risk of secondary spread of infection, and cyst content spillage may cause anaphylaxis. Choice A is incorrect because humans with cystic echinococcosis do not excreteE granulosuseggs in stool. Cystic echinococcosis is caused by infection with the larval stage of a tapeworm calledE granulosus. More than 1 million people annually are infected withE granulosusworldwide. Endemic regions include western China, Central Asia, South America, Mediterranean countries, and east Africa.1-3Cystic echinococcosis is rare in the US and typically occurs in immigrants from endemic countries.4 Definitive hosts forE granulosusare domestic or wild dogs and wolves (canids), who acquire the infection after eating animal organs containing hydatid cysts. Inside canids, the cysts develop into adult tapeworms, which shed eggs in their stool. Intermediate hosts, such as sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle, become infected after ingesting tapeworm eggs in contaminated soil.3Humans can become hosts through consumption of contaminated soil, food, or water, or after close contact with animal hosts.1After reaching the intestine,E granulosuseggs hatch and embryos penetrate the intestinal wall, migrating through blood or lymphatic vessels to organs, where they develop into hydatid cysts that gradually enlarge and produce more cysts.3,5 Approximately 70% of adults with cystic echinococcosis have liver cysts, and approximately 10% to 30% have pulmonary cysts.6In children, pulmonary cysts are the most common manifestation of cystic echinococcosis.7,8Less frequently, hyatid cysts develop in the brain, spleen, kidney, pancreas, and heart. Complications of cystic echinococcosis result from compression of adjacent organs, cyst rupture, superinfection, and immunoallergic reactions toEchinococcus, including urticaria, angioedema, and, rarely, anaphylaxis.8 Liver cysts typically grow slowly over many years in adults, but cysts often increase in size at a faster rate in the lung and in children.4,6,7Pulmonary cysts typically range from 1 cm to 20 cm, with giant cysts defined as having a diameter of 10 cm or greater.6Individuals with uncomplicated pulmonary hyatid cysts are typically asymptomatic, while those with complicated (ruptured or infected) cysts may experience cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, and fever.6Pulmonary cyst rupture can cause cough productive of salty-tasting fluid or membrane fragments, empyema, and hydropneumothorax.7 The diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis is made based on history, imaging, serology, and histology. Typical imaging findings are pulmonary cysts on chest radiographs or CT and liver cysts on abdominal ultrasound or CT. Detection of antibodies againstEchinococcuscan confirm the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis, although the sensitivity and specificity of serology each vary from 60% to 90%, and the sensitivity of serology is not well defined in children.4,7Eosinophilia occurs in approximately 25% of patients with confirmed cystic echinococcosis.9 Treatment for cystic echinococcosis depends on cyst size and location, presence or absence of complications, and availability of medical expertise and equipment.4Cure can be achieved by surgical resection of the cyst. Other treatments include PAIR (percutaneous puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration), antihelminth therapy, and watchful waiting for smaller cysts. Limited evidence is available regarding optimal drug therapy. However, albendazole or albendazole-praziquantel may be considered for patients with inoperable cysts in the liver, cysts in multiple organs, or isolated small or medium-sized cysts. Antihelminth therapy as an adjunct to surgery or interventional procedures decreased the risk of echinococcosis dissemination and recurrence.4,8,10Approximately 6.5% of patients experience a relapse after treatment for cystic echinococcosis.1 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay antibodies toEchinococcuswere detected, confirming the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis. Albendazole (15 mg/kg/d orally twice daily) was started 1 week before right upper lobectomy and continued for 5 months postoperatively. During surgery, a 12 × 12 × 8–cm pulmonary cyst was removed (Figure 2). Histopathology showed extensive necrosis and calcification, andE granulosuswas seen on hematoxylin and eosin stain. Five months after his initial surgery, the patient underwent laparotomy and complete removal of the 3 liver cysts, with no spillage of their contents. He was prescribed albendazole for 3 months postoperatively. When seen in the clinic 2 months after liver surgery, the patient had recovered well and an abdominal ultrasound showed no cyst recurrence.

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain serologic testing forE granulosusantibodies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that cysts in the lung and liver are highly suggestive of cystic echinococcosis. Organ biopsy (choices C and D) is not recommended because of the risk of secondary spread of infection, and cyst content spillage may cause anaphylaxis. Choice A is incorrect because humans with cystic echinococcosis do not excreteE granulosuseggs in stool. Cystic echinococcosis is caused by infection with the larval stage of a tapeworm calledE granulosus. More than 1 million people annually are infected withE granulosusworldwide. Endemic regions include western China, Central Asia, South America, Mediterranean countries, and east Africa.1-3Cystic echinococcosis is rare in the US and typically occurs in immigrants from endemic countries.4 Definitive hosts forE granulosusare domestic or wild dogs and wolves (canids), who acquire the infection after eating animal organs containing hydatid cysts. Inside canids, the cysts develop into adult tapeworms, which shed eggs in their stool. Intermediate hosts, such as sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle, become infected after ingesting tapeworm eggs in contaminated soil.3Humans can become hosts through consumption of contaminated soil, food, or water, or after close contact with animal hosts.1After reaching the intestine,E granulosuseggs hatch and embryos penetrate the intestinal wall, migrating through blood or lymphatic vessels to organs, where they develop into hydatid cysts that gradually enlarge and produce more cysts.3,5 Approximately 70% of adults with cystic echinococcosis have liver cysts, and approximately 10% to 30% have pulmonary cysts.6In children, pulmonary cysts are the most common manifestation of cystic echinococcosis.7,8Less frequently, hyatid cysts develop in the brain, spleen, kidney, pancreas, and heart. Complications of cystic echinococcosis result from compression of adjacent organs, cyst rupture, superinfection, and immunoallergic reactions toEchinococcus, including urticaria, angioedema, and, rarely, anaphylaxis.8 Liver cysts typically grow slowly over many years in adults, but cysts often increase in size at a faster rate in the lung and in children.4,6,7Pulmonary cysts typically range from 1 cm to 20 cm, with giant cysts defined as having a diameter of 10 cm or greater.6Individuals with uncomplicated pulmonary hyatid cysts are typically asymptomatic, while those with complicated (ruptured or infected) cysts may experience cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, and fever.6Pulmonary cyst rupture can cause cough productive of salty-tasting fluid or membrane fragments, empyema, and hydropneumothorax.7 The diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis is made based on history, imaging, serology, and histology. Typical imaging findings are pulmonary cysts on chest radiographs or CT and liver cysts on abdominal ultrasound or CT. Detection of antibodies againstEchinococcuscan confirm the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis, although the sensitivity and specificity of serology each vary from 60% to 90%, and the sensitivity of serology is not well defined in children.4,7Eosinophilia occurs in approximately 25% of patients with confirmed cystic echinococcosis.9 Treatment for cystic echinococcosis depends on cyst size and location, presence or absence of complications, and availability of medical expertise and equipment.4Cure can be achieved by surgical resection of the cyst. Other treatments include PAIR (percutaneous puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration), antihelminth therapy, and watchful waiting for smaller cysts. Limited evidence is available regarding optimal drug therapy. However, albendazole or albendazole-praziquantel may be considered for patients with inoperable cysts in the liver, cysts in multiple organs, or isolated small or medium-sized cysts. Antihelminth therapy as an adjunct to surgery or interventional procedures decreased the risk of echinococcosis dissemination and recurrence.4,8,10Approximately 6.5% of patients experience a relapse after treatment for cystic echinococcosis.1 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay antibodies toEchinococcuswere detected, confirming the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis. Albendazole (15 mg/kg/d orally twice daily) was started 1 week before right upper lobectomy and continued for 5 months postoperatively. During surgery, a 12 × 12 × 8–cm pulmonary cyst was removed (Figure 2). Histopathology showed extensive necrosis and calcification, andE granulosuswas seen on hematoxylin and eosin stain. Five months after his initial surgery, the patient underwent laparotomy and complete removal of the 3 liver cysts, with no spillage of their contents. He was prescribed albendazole for 3 months postoperatively. When seen in the clinic 2 months after liver surgery, the patient had recovered well and an abdominal ultrasound showed no cyst recurrence.

       hypotension or tachycardia."

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain serologic testing forE granulosusantibodies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that cysts in the lung and liver are highly suggestive of cystic echinococcosis. Organ biopsy (choices C and D) is not recommended because of the risk of secondary spread of infection, and cyst content spillage may cause anaphylaxis. Choice A is incorrect because humans with cystic echinococcosis do not excreteE granulosuseggs in stool. Cystic echinococcosis is caused by infection with the larval stage of a tapeworm calledE granulosus. More than 1 million people annually are infected withE granulosusworldwide. Endemic regions include western China, Central Asia, South America, Mediterranean countries, and east Africa.1-3Cystic echinococcosis is rare in the US and typically occurs in immigrants from endemic countries.4 Definitive hosts forE granulosusare domestic or wild dogs and wolves (canids), who acquire the infection after eating animal organs containing hydatid cysts. Inside canids, the cysts develop into adult tapeworms, which shed eggs in their stool. Intermediate hosts, such as sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle, become infected after ingesting tapeworm eggs in contaminated soil.3Humans can become hosts through consumption of contaminated soil, food, or water, or after close contact with animal hosts.1After reaching the intestine,E granulosuseggs hatch and embryos penetrate the intestinal wall, migrating through blood or lymphatic vessels to organs, where they develop into hydatid cysts that gradually enlarge and produce more cysts.3,5 Approximately 70% of adults with cystic echinococcosis have liver cysts, and approximately 10% to 30% have pulmonary cysts.6In children, pulmonary cysts are the most common manifestation of cystic echinococcosis.7,8Less frequently, hyatid cysts develop in the brain, spleen, kidney, pancreas, and heart. Complications of cystic echinococcosis result from compression of adjacent organs, cyst rupture, superinfection, and immunoallergic reactions toEchinococcus, including urticaria, angioedema, and, rarely, anaphylaxis.8 Liver cysts typically grow slowly over many years in adults, but cysts often increase in size at a faster rate in the lung and in children.4,6,7Pulmonary cysts typically range from 1 cm to 20 cm, with giant cysts defined as having a diameter of 10 cm or greater.6Individuals with uncomplicated pulmonary hyatid cysts are typically asymptomatic, while those with complicated (ruptured or infected) cysts may experience cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, and fever.6Pulmonary cyst rupture can cause cough productive of salty-tasting fluid or membrane fragments, empyema, and hydropneumothorax.7 The diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis is made based on history, imaging, serology, and histology. Typical imaging findings are pulmonary cysts on chest radiographs or CT and liver cysts on abdominal ultrasound or CT. Detection of antibodies againstEchinococcuscan confirm the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis, although the sensitivity and specificity of serology each vary from 60% to 90%, and the sensitivity of serology is not well defined in children.4,7Eosinophilia occurs in approximately 25% of patients with confirmed cystic echinococcosis.9 Treatment for cystic echinococcosis depends on cyst size and location, presence or absence of complications, and availability of medical expertise and equipment.4Cure can be achieved by surgical resection of the cyst. Other treatments include PAIR (percutaneous puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration), antihelminth therapy, and watchful waiting for smaller cysts. Limited evidence is available regarding optimal drug therapy. However, albendazole or albendazole-praziquantel may be considered for patients with inoperable cysts in the liver, cysts in multiple organs, or isolated small or medium-sized cysts. Antihelminth therapy as an adjunct to surgery or interventional procedures decreased the risk of echinococcosis dissemination and recurrence.4,8,10Approximately 6.5% of patients experience a relapse after treatment for cystic echinococcosis.1 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay antibodies toEchinococcuswere detected, confirming the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis. Albendazole (15 mg/kg/d orally twice daily) was started 1 week before right upper lobectomy and continued for 5 months postoperatively. During surgery, a 12 × 12 × 8–cm pulmonary cyst was removed (Figure 2). Histopathology showed extensive necrosis and calcification, andE granulosuswas seen on hematoxylin and eosin stain. Five months after his initial surgery, the patient underwent laparotomy and complete removal of the 3 liver cysts, with no spillage of their contents. He was prescribed albendazole for 3 months postoperatively. When seen in the clinic 2 months after liver surgery, the patient had recovered well and an abdominal ultrasound showed no cyst recurrence.

Obtain serologic testing forE granulosusantibodies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that cysts in the lung and liver are highly suggestive of cystic echinococcosis. Organ biopsy (choices C and D) is not recommended because of the risk of secondary spread of infection, and cyst content spillage may cause anaphylaxis. Choice A is incorrect because humans with cystic echinococcosis do not excreteE granulosuseggs in stool. Cystic echinococcosis is caused by infection with the larval stage of a tapeworm calledE granulosus. More than 1 million people annually are infected withE granulosusworldwide. Endemic regions include western China, Central Asia, South America, Mediterranean countries, and east Africa.1-3Cystic echinococcosis is rare in the US and typically occurs in immigrants from endemic countries.4 Definitive hosts forE granulosusare domestic or wild dogs and wolves (canids), who acquire the infection after eating animal organs containing hydatid cysts. Inside canids, the cysts develop into adult tapeworms, which shed eggs in their stool. Intermediate hosts, such as sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle, become infected after ingesting tapeworm eggs in contaminated soil.3Humans can become hosts through consumption of contaminated soil, food, or water, or after close contact with animal hosts.1After reaching the intestine,E granulosuseggs hatch and embryos penetrate the intestinal wall, migrating through blood or lymphatic vessels to organs, where they develop into hydatid cysts that gradually enlarge and produce more cysts.3,5 Approximately 70% of adults with cystic echinococcosis have liver cysts, and approximately 10% to 30% have pulmonary cysts.6In children, pulmonary cysts are the most common manifestation of cystic echinococcosis.7,8Less frequently, hyatid cysts develop in the brain, spleen, kidney, pancreas, and heart. Complications of cystic echinococcosis result from compression of adjacent organs, cyst rupture, superinfection, and immunoallergic reactions toEchinococcus, including urticaria, angioedema, and, rarely, anaphylaxis.8 Liver cysts typically grow slowly over many years in adults, but cysts often increase in size at a faster rate in the lung and in children.4,6,7Pulmonary cysts typically range from 1 cm to 20 cm, with giant cysts defined as having a diameter of 10 cm or greater.6Individuals with uncomplicated pulmonary hyatid cysts are typically asymptomatic, while those with complicated (ruptured or infected) cysts may experience cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, and fever.6Pulmonary cyst rupture can cause cough productive of salty-tasting fluid or membrane fragments, empyema, and hydropneumothorax.7 The diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis is made based on history, imaging, serology, and histology. Typical imaging findings are pulmonary cysts on chest radiographs or CT and liver cysts on abdominal ultrasound or CT. Detection of antibodies againstEchinococcuscan confirm the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis, although the sensitivity and specificity of serology each vary from 60% to 90%, and the sensitivity of serology is not well defined in children.4,7Eosinophilia occurs in approximately 25% of patients with confirmed cystic echinococcosis.9 Treatment for cystic echinococcosis depends on cyst size and location, presence or absence of complications, and availability of medical expertise and equipment.4Cure can be achieved by surgical resection of the cyst. Other treatments include PAIR (percutaneous puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration), antihelminth therapy, and watchful waiting for smaller cysts. Limited evidence is available regarding optimal drug therapy. However, albendazole or albendazole-praziquantel may be considered for patients with inoperable cysts in the liver, cysts in multiple organs, or isolated small or medium-sized cysts. Antihelminth therapy as an adjunct to surgery or interventional procedures decreased the risk of echinococcosis dissemination and recurrence.4,8,10Approximately 6.5% of patients experience a relapse after treatment for cystic echinococcosis.1 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay antibodies toEchinococcuswere detected, confirming the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis. Albendazole (15 mg/kg/d orally twice daily) was started 1 week before right upper lobectomy and continued for 5 months postoperatively. During surgery, a 12 × 12 × 8–cm pulmonary cyst was removed (Figure 2). Histopathology showed extensive necrosis and calcification, andE granulosuswas seen on hematoxylin and eosin stain. Five months after his initial surgery, the patient underwent laparotomy and complete removal of the 3 liver cysts, with no spillage of their contents. He was prescribed albendazole for 3 months postoperatively. When seen in the clinic 2 months after liver surgery, the patient had recovered well and an abdominal ultrasound showed no cyst recurrence.

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain serologic testing forE granulosusantibodies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that cysts in the lung and liver are highly suggestive of cystic echinococcosis. Organ biopsy (choices C and D) is not recommended because of the risk of secondary spread of infection, and cyst content spillage may cause anaphylaxis. Choice A is incorrect because humans with cystic echinococcosis do not excreteE granulosuseggs in stool. Cystic echinococcosis is caused by infection with the larval stage of a tapeworm calledE granulosus. More than 1 million people annually are infected withE granulosusworldwide. Endemic regions include western China, Central Asia, South America, Mediterranean countries, and east Africa.1-3Cystic echinococcosis is rare in the US and typically occurs in immigrants from endemic countries.4 Definitive hosts forE granulosusare domestic or wild dogs and wolves (canids), who acquire the infection after eating animal organs containing hydatid cysts. Inside canids, the cysts develop into adult tapeworms, which shed eggs in their stool. Intermediate hosts, such as sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle, become infected after ingesting tapeworm eggs in contaminated soil.3Humans can become hosts through consumption of contaminated soil, food, or water, or after close contact with animal hosts.1After reaching the intestine,E granulosuseggs hatch and embryos penetrate the intestinal wall, migrating through blood or lymphatic vessels to organs, where they develop into hydatid cysts that gradually enlarge and produce more cysts.3,5 Approximately 70% of adults with cystic echinococcosis have liver cysts, and approximately 10% to 30% have pulmonary cysts.6In children, pulmonary cysts are the most common manifestation of cystic echinococcosis.7,8Less frequently, hyatid cysts develop in the brain, spleen, kidney, pancreas, and heart. Complications of cystic echinococcosis result from compression of adjacent organs, cyst rupture, superinfection, and immunoallergic reactions toEchinococcus, including urticaria, angioedema, and, rarely, anaphylaxis.8 Liver cysts typically grow slowly over many years in adults, but cysts often increase in size at a faster rate in the lung and in children.4,6,7Pulmonary cysts typically range from 1 cm to 20 cm, with giant cysts defined as having a diameter of 10 cm or greater.6Individuals with uncomplicated pulmonary hyatid cysts are typically asymptomatic, while those with complicated (ruptured or infected) cysts may experience cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, and fever.6Pulmonary cyst rupture can cause cough productive of salty-tasting fluid or membrane fragments, empyema, and hydropneumothorax.7 The diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis is made based on history, imaging, serology, and histology. Typical imaging findings are pulmonary cysts on chest radiographs or CT and liver cysts on abdominal ultrasound or CT. Detection of antibodies againstEchinococcuscan confirm the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis, although the sensitivity and specificity of serology each vary from 60% to 90%, and the sensitivity of serology is not well defined in children.4,7Eosinophilia occurs in approximately 25% of patients with confirmed cystic echinococcosis.9 Treatment for cystic echinococcosis depends on cyst size and location, presence or absence of complications, and availability of medical expertise and equipment.4Cure can be achieved by surgical resection of the cyst. Other treatments include PAIR (percutaneous puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration), antihelminth therapy, and watchful waiting for smaller cysts. Limited evidence is available regarding optimal drug therapy. However, albendazole or albendazole-praziquantel may be considered for patients with inoperable cysts in the liver, cysts in multiple organs, or isolated small or medium-sized cysts. Antihelminth therapy as an adjunct to surgery or interventional procedures decreased the risk of echinococcosis dissemination and recurrence.4,8,10Approximately 6.5% of patients experience a relapse after treatment for cystic echinococcosis.1 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay antibodies toEchinococcuswere detected, confirming the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis. Albendazole (15 mg/kg/d orally twice daily) was started 1 week before right upper lobectomy and continued for 5 months postoperatively. During surgery, a 12 × 12 × 8–cm pulmonary cyst was removed (Figure 2). Histopathology showed extensive necrosis and calcification, andE granulosuswas seen on hematoxylin and eosin stain. Five months after his initial surgery, the patient underwent laparotomy and complete removal of the 3 liver cysts, with no spillage of their contents. He was prescribed albendazole for 3 months postoperatively. When seen in the clinic 2 months after liver surgery, the patient had recovered well and an abdominal ultrasound showed no cyst recurrence.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain serologic testing forE granulosusantibodies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that cysts in the lung and liver are highly suggestive of cystic echinococcosis. Organ biopsy (choices C and D) is not recommended because of the risk of secondary spread of infection, and cyst content spillage may cause anaphylaxis. Choice A is incorrect because humans with cystic echinococcosis do not excreteE granulosuseggs in stool. Cystic echinococcosis is caused by infection with the larval stage of a tapeworm calledE granulosus. More than 1 million people annually are infected withE granulosusworldwide. Endemic regions include western China, Central Asia, South America, Mediterranean countries, and east Africa.1-3Cystic echinococcosis is rare in the US and typically occurs in immigrants from endemic countries.4 Definitive hosts forE granulosusare domestic or wild dogs and wolves (canids), who acquire the infection after eating animal organs containing hydatid cysts. Inside canids, the cysts develop into adult tapeworms, which shed eggs in their stool. Intermediate hosts, such as sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle, become infected after ingesting tapeworm eggs in contaminated soil.3Humans can become hosts through consumption of contaminated soil, food, or water, or after close contact with animal hosts.1After reaching the intestine,E granulosuseggs hatch and embryos penetrate the intestinal wall, migrating through blood or lymphatic vessels to organs, where they develop into hydatid cysts that gradually enlarge and produce more cysts.3,5 Approximately 70% of adults with cystic echinococcosis have liver cysts, and approximately 10% to 30% have pulmonary cysts.6In children, pulmonary cysts are the most common manifestation of cystic echinococcosis.7,8Less frequently, hyatid cysts develop in the brain, spleen, kidney, pancreas, and heart. Complications of cystic echinococcosis result from compression of adjacent organs, cyst rupture, superinfection, and immunoallergic reactions toEchinococcus, including urticaria, angioedema, and, rarely, anaphylaxis.8 Liver cysts typically grow slowly over many years in adults, but cysts often increase in size at a faster rate in the lung and in children.4,6,7Pulmonary cysts typically range from 1 cm to 20 cm, with giant cysts defined as having a diameter of 10 cm or greater.6Individuals with uncomplicated pulmonary hyatid cysts are typically asymptomatic, while those with complicated (ruptured or infected) cysts may experience cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, and fever.6Pulmonary cyst rupture can cause cough productive of salty-tasting fluid or membrane fragments, empyema, and hydropneumothorax.7 The diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis is made based on history, imaging, serology, and histology. Typical imaging findings are pulmonary cysts on chest radiographs or CT and liver cysts on abdominal ultrasound or CT. Detection of antibodies againstEchinococcuscan confirm the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis, although the sensitivity and specificity of serology each vary from 60% to 90%, and the sensitivity of serology is not well defined in children.4,7Eosinophilia occurs in approximately 25% of patients with confirmed cystic echinococcosis.9 Treatment for cystic echinococcosis depends on cyst size and location, presence or absence of complications, and availability of medical expertise and equipment.4Cure can be achieved by surgical resection of the cyst. Other treatments include PAIR (percutaneous puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration), antihelminth therapy, and watchful waiting for smaller cysts. Limited evidence is available regarding optimal drug therapy. However, albendazole or albendazole-praziquantel may be considered for patients with inoperable cysts in the liver, cysts in multiple organs, or isolated small or medium-sized cysts. Antihelminth therapy as an adjunct to surgery or interventional procedures decreased the risk of echinococcosis dissemination and recurrence.4,8,10Approximately 6.5% of patients experience a relapse after treatment for cystic echinococcosis.1 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay antibodies toEchinococcuswere detected, confirming the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis. Albendazole (15 mg/kg/d orally twice daily) was started 1 week before right upper lobectomy and continued for 5 months postoperatively. During surgery, a 12 × 12 × 8–cm pulmonary cyst was removed (Figure 2). Histopathology showed extensive necrosis and calcification, andE granulosuswas seen on hematoxylin and eosin stain. Five months after his initial surgery, the patient underwent laparotomy and complete removal of the 3 liver cysts, with no spillage of their contents. He was prescribed albendazole for 3 months postoperatively. When seen in the clinic 2 months after liver surgery, the patient had recovered well and an abdominal ultrasound showed no cyst recurrence.

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain serologic testing forE granulosusantibodies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that cysts in the lung and liver are highly suggestive of cystic echinococcosis. Organ biopsy (choices C and D) is not recommended because of the risk of secondary spread of infection, and cyst content spillage may cause anaphylaxis. Choice A is incorrect because humans with cystic echinococcosis do not excreteE granulosuseggs in stool. Cystic echinococcosis is caused by infection with the larval stage of a tapeworm calledE granulosus. More than 1 million people annually are infected withE granulosusworldwide. Endemic regions include western China, Central Asia, South America, Mediterranean countries, and east Africa.1-3Cystic echinococcosis is rare in the US and typically occurs in immigrants from endemic countries.4 Definitive hosts forE granulosusare domestic or wild dogs and wolves (canids), who acquire the infection after eating animal organs containing hydatid cysts. Inside canids, the cysts develop into adult tapeworms, which shed eggs in their stool. Intermediate hosts, such as sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle, become infected after ingesting tapeworm eggs in contaminated soil.3Humans can become hosts through consumption of contaminated soil, food, or water, or after close contact with animal hosts.1After reaching the intestine,E granulosuseggs hatch and embryos penetrate the intestinal wall, migrating through blood or lymphatic vessels to organs, where they develop into hydatid cysts that gradually enlarge and produce more cysts.3,5 Approximately 70% of adults with cystic echinococcosis have liver cysts, and approximately 10% to 30% have pulmonary cysts.6In children, pulmonary cysts are the most common manifestation of cystic echinococcosis.7,8Less frequently, hyatid cysts develop in the brain, spleen, kidney, pancreas, and heart. Complications of cystic echinococcosis result from compression of adjacent organs, cyst rupture, superinfection, and immunoallergic reactions toEchinococcus, including urticaria, angioedema, and, rarely, anaphylaxis.8 Liver cysts typically grow slowly over many years in adults, but cysts often increase in size at a faster rate in the lung and in children.4,6,7Pulmonary cysts typically range from 1 cm to 20 cm, with giant cysts defined as having a diameter of 10 cm or greater.6Individuals with uncomplicated pulmonary hyatid cysts are typically asymptomatic, while those with complicated (ruptured or infected) cysts may experience cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, and fever.6Pulmonary cyst rupture can cause cough productive of salty-tasting fluid or membrane fragments, empyema, and hydropneumothorax.7 The diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis is made based on history, imaging, serology, and histology. Typical imaging findings are pulmonary cysts on chest radiographs or CT and liver cysts on abdominal ultrasound or CT. Detection of antibodies againstEchinococcuscan confirm the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis, although the sensitivity and specificity of serology each vary from 60% to 90%, and the sensitivity of serology is not well defined in children.4,7Eosinophilia occurs in approximately 25% of patients with confirmed cystic echinococcosis.9 Treatment for cystic echinococcosis depends on cyst size and location, presence or absence of complications, and availability of medical expertise and equipment.4Cure can be achieved by surgical resection of the cyst. Other treatments include PAIR (percutaneous puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration), antihelminth therapy, and watchful waiting for smaller cysts. Limited evidence is available regarding optimal drug therapy. However, albendazole or albendazole-praziquantel may be considered for patients with inoperable cysts in the liver, cysts in multiple organs, or isolated small or medium-sized cysts. Antihelminth therapy as an adjunct to surgery or interventional procedures decreased the risk of echinococcosis dissemination and recurrence.4,8,10Approximately 6.5% of patients experience a relapse after treatment for cystic echinococcosis.1 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay antibodies toEchinococcuswere detected, confirming the diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis. Albendazole (15 mg/kg/d orally twice daily) was started 1 week before right upper lobectomy and continued for 5 months postoperatively. During surgery, a 12 × 12 × 8–cm pulmonary cyst was removed (Figure 2). Histopathology showed extensive necrosis and calcification, andE granulosuswas seen on hematoxylin and eosin stain. Five months after his initial surgery, the patient underwent laparotomy and complete removal of the 3 liver cysts, with no spillage of their contents. He was prescribed albendazole for 3 months postoperatively. When seen in the clinic 2 months after liver surgery, the patient had recovered well and an abdominal ultrasound showed no cyst recurrence.
